text: Does the delegate of Canada not realise that by this resolution, the authority over entire operations pertaining to your goal of preventing recruitment into the mafia is left in the hands of P5 countries, who, at many occasions, have been shown not to be the most trustworthy countries, and that banking on them has the potential for the complete failure of your resolution?

Notably in 2023, the DIA had carried out mass action against mafias such as Camorra and 'Ndrangheta. Why hasn't there been any more action that at the very least, we know of that has happened between 2024 and 2025?

Does the delegate of the United States agree that stopping the Houthis and closing off Yemen as a weapons and drugs backdoor is critical to ensuring that the mafia has no more routes to import illegal goods through?

El Chapo's Sinaloa cartel makes billions of USD per annum in the drug trade. Simultaneously reports have also shown that Mexico is used as a hiding place for mafias such as the 'Ndrangheta. Seeing as these cartels are also trafficking drugs and weapons to the Sicilian mafia, does the delegate agree that Mexico is no longer a mere 'transit country', but rather a fully-fledged mafia state?

Colombia is the largest producer of cocaine worldwide. Since locally-based cartels often times work closely with mafias such as 'Ndrangheta and Camorra, what existing legal measures, and if so, proposed legislation exists to shut off the Colombian cocaine farm to non-state actors?

In 2019, Saudi Arabia was placed on a blacklist by the EU referring to money laundering and terrorist financing, requiring EU banks to conduct intensive checks on funds coming through Saudi Arabia. This includes money that was laundered in the interest of the Italian mafia, considering that Italian mafia bosses have admitted to using the Middle East as a hub for money laundering. Why has the Saudi government, of whom was also indicted for money laundering in 2017, not tightened enforcement of money laundering legislation despite its already established anti-corruption body and legislature related to the crime, considering that 5.74% of its GDP comes under fire in relation to the crime?

The Cosa Nostra and Camorra, as per DIA reports, were shown to have used Chinese underground banking to transfer 'dirty money' and assets related to illicit trafficking. Notably, in 2024, Italian financial police had uncovered approximately 2 billion euros in dirty money that was said to have been processed using Chinese shadow banking. Why did the Chinese government take action against crimes that took place within its own territory, given the so secure nature of Chinese finance?

The Russian Federation is known as a primary route for Afghan heroin to travel through in order to reach Europe, where it is distributed and exploited by mafias. Albeit that arrests were seldom made, Russia remains a primary route for Afghan heroin (the Balkan route). Why hasn't there been more action towards securing the border as for heroin to be unable to travel via Russia?

As per UN Security Council reports, the Iranian government is both a supplier of weapons for, and a staunch supporter of the Houthis, a terrorist group, who in effect allow a backdoor for the mafia for weapons and arms trade, with Iranian ships, as per the same report having been parked in Al-Hudaydah. Does the Iranian government deny that its support of the Houthi regime enables both the mafia's backdoor in Yemen and terrorism?

In 2021, the mafia boss Raffaele Imperiale was arrested in Dubai. He had admitted to using the UAE as a hub for money laundering for what reports would call 'a very long time.' Considering that reports like this have been persistent in placing the UAE into the mire of being dubbed a 'criminal safe haven,' why hasn't there been more action against Italian mafia bosses such as Imperiale who covertly operate in your jurisdiction, and why not earlier, as Imperiale had moved to the UAE back in 2013?

Djibouti loans land to 7 different militaries, one of them being China, who has been accused of processing Mafia payments via its underground banking system, simultaneously conducting a campaign against these funds that can be called mediocre at best, especially as Italian authorities intercepted the aforementioned Chinese funds. What does the delegate of Djibouti propose to prevent its ports along the Bab-el-Mandeb strait from becoming the next Al-Hudaydah for the mafia?

Malta has a notoriously corrupt government which has been repeatedly underscored in multiple reports from Transparency International, an organisation dedicated to mitigating global corruption. If the delegate of Malta attempts to fix the mafia crisis plaguing its territories, shouldn't it first tackle the issues that plague its government with the inability to act against these mafias through measures such as anti-corruption legislature?

Follow up if Malta blames it on the mafia: Does this delegate not realize that in 2015, the former PM, Joseph Muscat, was shown to have privatised a number of hospitals in Malta, for his own personal gain as evidenced in the contents of leaked emails between the PM and the Swiss firm Acutor who reimbursed him after the enactment of the privatization?

The delegation of Colombia suggests for soft measures, advocating against these hard measures despite the fact that those measures have failed consistently against its own cartel. When faced with this inefficiency, isn't Colombia's proposal to a degree, hypocritical, considering their desire to quench the cartel - especially as Colombia itself has used hard measures such as SWAT teams on these cartels?
Colombia failed to eradicate cartels using soft power. Your proposal's hypocritical.
Does the delegate of Japan agree that the intervention by the NATO Maritime Interdiction Force around the Red Sea is critical to ensuring the collapse of mafia groups?

The delegation of Canada expresses its displeasure with the hardline anti-mafia motion. Does this delegation, in effect, believe that their idea of a valid solution is solely to prevent the recruitment into the mafia, forgoing the fact that the mafia itself must be dealt with as well?
Does this delegate believe that an investment of 800M USD, funds seized from the Ndrangheta, would be a sufficient amount for maintaining the Delulu body?

On the 6th of July 2025, the Liberian-flagged ship Eternity C was sunk in the Red Sea, notably after the United States had reduced operations in the area, with the departure of USS Harry S. Truman on the 17th of May 2025. Does the delegate of the United States admit that its reduction of naval operations in the area is only allowing the Houthis to continue their terrorist operations with near-guaranteed impunity?

In 2009, a crew of four pirates led by Abduwali Muse hijacked the Maersk Alabama for financial gain, proving piracy to be a profitable industry, especially considering that around that 2010 the average ransom paid was around 54 million USD, an all time high. Pairing that with recent Somali pirate attacks on Yemeni vessels, does the delegate of Somalia believe that it is crucial to implement stronger naval measures around the coasts of Somalia and Yemen, and if so, propose any measures in doing so?

Seeing as the Suez Canal has been impacted by the 2023-2025 Red Sea crisis, what measures could the delegate propose to ensure the safety of the Red Sea, especially considering the fact that Egypt is one of the strongest countries in Africa?

Notably in 2019, the Saudi government led a coalition to combat the Houthis, a major ally of maritime pirates. The coalition's attacks on Yemeni soil led to numerous noncombatant casualties, destroying Yemen's economy and creating what is probably the biggest opportunity for the Houthis and Somali pirates to attack. So when the delegate of Saudi Arabia condemns piracy, is it just a cover-up for their war crimes?

The UK supplied 97 billion GBP worth of arms to the Saudi coalition (8.2B to Saudi Arabia alone) which bombed Yemen, creating what the UK's own CAAT report dubs 'the world's largest humanitarian crisis, only fuelling the birth of today's Houthi-led piracy crisis. By condemning piracy and Houthi involvement in the Red Sea, isn't this to a degree, hypocritical, as the UK only benefited economically from the war in Yemen?'

Nearly 60% of Chinese trade flows through the Houthi-threatened Red Sea. However, on numerous occasions, China decided to abstain from voting on key resolutions such as 2722, which demanded the Houthi cease attacks on Red Sea vessels, including on a Chinese oil tanker, which was struck by Houthi missiles in 2024. What exactly is China trying to protect by refusing to vote on resolutions that only affect it positively?

80% of Indian trade flows through the Red Sea, but amidst the ongoing Red Sea crisis, the Indian government has not taken any action to combat the crisis perpetuated by Houthi terrorism, despite their trade practically relying on the body of water. Simultaneously, India imports 13% of its oil from Iran which is the Houthis' strongest regional supporter, while sending warships to Somalia as their own vessels are attacked by the Houthis. Is this hypocrisy, cowardice, or a secret trade agreement?

Despite the fact that India is plagued with internal issues such as the caste system, corruption, and its struggling infrastructure, India is heavily involved in the action against piracy off the coast of Somalialand. How can the Indian government expect to solve the issues of other countries despite failing to solve its own internal crises?

As per a CSIS estimate, 32% of Japanese imports and 25% of Japanese imports flow through the Red Sea, which, not to reiterate the obvious, is under attack by Houthi terrorists. Since such a significant amount of Japanese trade is reliant on the Red Sea, and a Japanese-operated cargo ship was hijacked by the Houthis in 2023, why hasn't there been more action from Japan aside from mere condemnations?

In 2018, the Russian delegation at the UNSC vetoed a resolution aimed at blocking Iran from supplying weapons to the Houthis. Today, those same weapons that Russia allowed to flow arm terrorists with the capabilities to attack civilian vessels passing through the Red Sea. Does the delegate of Russia still believe that this veto 'preserved regional stability', or that it guaranteed the next generation of terrorists to work scot-free, with the blood on Russia's hands?

Pakistan is conducting anti-piracy operations off the coast of Somalia, but in 2024, it decided not to act on the Red Sea crisis off the coast of Yemen, against Houthi insurgents attacking civilian vessels. By doing this, is Pakistan attempting to avoid Iran's ire while sailors suffer, especially considering that Pakistan's close ally, Djibouti is situated only 32km from the coast of Houthi-occupied Yemen?

The government of Iran is known to provide funds to the Houthi insurgency, an internationally designated terrorist group. This is in violation of UNSC resolution 2462. Does the delegate of Iran condone the unspeakable acts of terror that have been committed against innocent sailors by the funding of the Houthis, and in turn, Somali pirates?

How can we ensure that the proposed military interventions and the enforcement operations in the Red Sea are carried out in the way that respects the sovereignty and territorial integrity of the coastal states and residents?

What mechanisms can be put in place to ensure transparency and accountability of the distribution of military equipment and the resources to the affected regions, how can we prevent diversion or misuse of these assets?

The resolution proposes to use satellite imagery and data-sharing to track and dismantle pirate mother ships. What privacy safeguards can be implemented to protect the right of the innocent manners whose movements may be monitored?
How would the resolution ensure the efficiency of re-allocation of money in clause 4c given that corruption is rampant?

The resolution calls for the deployment of enhanced drone surveillance to track pirate motherships. Can you provide more details on the safeguards that will be in place to ensure these drones are used responsibly and do not infringe on the privacy of legitimate mariners?

Clause 4 outlines plans for the rehabilitation and reintegration of captured pirates. Can you elaborate on the specific training and education programs that will be offered, and how you will ensure these initiatives are truly effective in preventing recidivism?

Clause 5 mentions the provision of "short-term aids" such as funds, technology, and medical equipment. Can you clarify how the distribution and utilization of these resources will be monitored to ensure transparency and prevent misuse?
